tx.t: In this lecture I will describe how honeybees live and why they matter so much to farmers. A single summer hive can contain up to sixty thousand bees, but only one queen.

Worker bees live for only about six weeks in summer, and they spend their lives doing different jobs, from cleaning the hive to collecting nectar. In its whole life, one worker produces only about one-twelfth of a teaspoon of honey.

Bees tell each other where food is by dancing. The angle of the dance shows the direction, and its length shows the distance. Many crops, such as almonds and apples, depend on bees to carry pollen from flower to flower.

tx.t: Today I would like to describe a bike-sharing scheme in the town of Fenwick. It began in two thousand and nine with six hundred and fifty-two bikes, placed at stations around the centre.
Use grew quickly. Within three years the number of journeys had risen by seventy-one per cent, and on a busy day there were more than twenty-two thousand trips.
The scheme soon met a serious problem: too few bikes in the hills. The council solved it with a van that moves bikes uphill every morning.
Today, a ride costs three pounds for the first half hour, and the first fifteen minutes are free for residents.

bikes being left in the wrong places
marked parking zones with a small fine for leaving a bike outside them
a tracking system fixed inside each frame
a mobile app that shows where bikes are available

tx.t: Let me tell you something about the history and the economics of coffee. According to legend, coffee was discovered in Ethiopia by a goat herder called Kaldi, who noticed that his goats became lively after eating the berries.

By the fifteenth century, coffee was grown in Yemen, and it then spread to Turkey and Europe. There are two main kinds of coffee, Arabica and Robusta, and about sixty per cent of the world's coffee is Arabica.
Brazil produces about one third of the world's coffee, more than any other country. People around the world drink about two billion cups of coffee every day.

tx.t: Researchers at the University of Alderton carried out a study in twenty eighteen to find out how students prepare for exams. They followed one hundred and thirty-two students over four weeks.
On average, the students studied for seven hours a day. However, only fifty-one per cent of them used any planned method.
The students who used the method of sleeping at least eight hours made fewer mistakes in the test. The researchers concluded that how you study may matter more than how long you study.

tx.t: This lecture is about the International Space Station, or ISS. The ISS orbits about four hundred kilometres above the Earth.
It travels at roughly twenty-eight thousand kilometres an hour, so it circles the Earth about every ninety minutes. That means the crew sees about sixteen sunrises every day.
People have lived on board continuously since November two thousand. Without gravity, muscles and bones become weaker, so astronauts exercise for about two hours a day.
The first human in space was the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin, in nineteen sixty-one.

tx.t: This morning we are going to look at some basic facts about the Moon. The Moon is about three hundred and eighty-four thousand kilometres from the Earth.
It takes about twenty-seven days to orbit the Earth once. The same side of the Moon always faces us, because its rotation takes exactly as long as its orbit.
The Moon is about a quarter of the width of the Earth. Gravity on the Moon is only about one-sixth of gravity on Earth.
In nineteen sixty-nine, Apollo Eleven became the first mission to land humans there.

tx.t: Today I would like to talk about the Silk Road, one of the greatest trade networks in history. It was not a single road but a network of routes connecting China with the Mediterranean.
The main routes were more than six thousand kilometres long. The Chinese envoy Zhang Qian travelled west around one hundred and thirty BC and helped to open the routes.

Besides silk, merchants carried spices, paper, glass and precious stones, and also ideas and religions. The routes became less important when sea trade grew cheaper in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.
